title: Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia
authors: Allentoft M.E., Sikora M., Sjogren K.-G., ... Willerslev E.
ask_addressed: Open and quote the primary aDNA and phylogenetic papers on Indo-European origins: Haak et al. 2015, Allentoft et al. 2015, Damgaard et al. 2018, Narasimhan et al. 2019, Bouckaert et al. 2012, Heggarty et al. 2023, Lazaridis et al. on the Anatolian question. Use bioRxiv, Europe PMC, PMC, institutional repositories, or Crossref/Unpaywall to find open copies.
quote: Our findings are consistent with the hypothesized spread of Indo-European languages during the Early Bronze Age.
summary: 101 low-coverage Bronze Age genomes show large-scale migrations and replacements across Eurasia; the authors call the pattern consistent with an Early Bronze Age spread of Indo-European languages.
limits: Only the abstract was opened (full text paywalled). 'Consistent with' is the authors' own hedge: the paper measures ancestry, not language. Companion to Haak et al. Verifier: strand changed from people/documented to language/inferred because the quoted passage is a hedged language claim; DNA shows ancestry, not language.

strand.what: Indo-European languages (authors say findings are 'consistent with' an Early Bronze Age spread; the migrations themselves are in the abstract's preceding sentence)

title: 137 ancient human genomes from across the Eurasian steppes
authors: Damgaard P.B., Marchi N., Rasmussen S., ... Willerslev E.
ask_addressed: Open and quote the primary aDNA and phylogenetic papers on Indo-European origins: Haak et al. 2015, Allentoft et al. 2015, Damgaard et al. 2018, Narasimhan et al. 2019, Bouckaert et al. 2012, Heggarty et al. 2023, Lazaridis et al. on the Anatolian question. quote: transformed the Eurasian steppes from being inhabited by Indo-European speakers of largely West Eurasian ancestry to the mostly Turkic-speaking groups of the present day
summary: Covers the steppe after the Bronze Age migrations; shows Scythian, Xiongnu, Hun and later groups mixing so that West Eurasian-ancestry Indo-European speakers gave way to East Asian-ancestry Turkic speakers.
limits: Only the abstract was opened (paywalled). It is about steppe history after the Indo-European dispersal, so it is context for the steppe side, not a test of the homeland. Language assignments rest on the historical record, not the DNA. Verifier: directness lowered from documented to inferred because the strand ties ancestry turnover to a language turnover, and the language side rests on the historical record.

strand.what: ancestry turnover linked to a language turnover

Use bioRxiv, Europe PMC, PMC, institutional repositories, or Crossref/Unpaywall to find open copies.
quote: tracking a movement of people that affected both regions and that likely spread the unique shared features shared between Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic languages
summary: 523 ancient genomes: Steppe pastoralist ancestry reached South Asia after ~4000 years ago with the same profile as Bronze Age eastern Europe, read as the carrier of Indo-Iranian languages; Iranian-related ancestry is argued to be less plausible.
limits: Argues Steppe ancestry is the more plausible vehicle; the abstract itself notes 'There is no ancient DNA yet for the ANI and ASI' (inferred statistically). Language link is inferential. Says nothing on the Anatolian branch.

title: Mapping the origins and expansion of the Indo-European language family
authors: Bouckaert R., Lemey P., Dunn M., Greenhill S.J., Alekseyenko A.V., Drummond A.J., Gray R.D., Suchard M.A., Atkinson Q.D.
ask_addressed: Open and quote the primary aDNA and phylogenetic papers on Indo-European origins: Haak et al. 2015, Allentoft et al. 2015, Damgaard et al. 2018, Narasimhan et al. 2019, Bouckaert et al. 2012, Heggarty et al. 2023, Lazaridis et al. on the Anatolian question. Use bioRxiv, Europe PMC, PMC, institutional repositories, or Crossref/Unpaywall to find open copies.
quote: We find decisive support for an Anatolian over a steppe origin.
summary: Bayesian phylogeographic model of vocabulary from 103 languages favours an Anatolian root and a farming-linked expansion beginning in the 9th millennium BP.
limits: Superseded in part by later work (Chang et al. 2015 and Heggarty et al. 2023 get different roots; Heggarty uses ancestry-enabled trees and a new cognate database). The paper's own PMC page notes a published correction (Science 342:1446). Authors include proponents of the Anatolian view.

strand.to: Europe and the rest of the Indo-European area

quote: it does not rule out an initial homeland south of the Caucasus, with a subsequent branch northward onto the steppe and then across Europe.
summary: New core-vocabulary database and ancestry-enabled trees give a root of ~8120 yr B.P., which the authors say is not consistent with the Steppe hypothesis; they propose a hybrid homeland south of the Caucasus with a later steppe branch.
limits: Only the abstract on the repository page was opened (science.org returned 403; the University Jaume I copy sits behind an Anubis bot wall and was not used). Criticised by Kassian and Starostin 2025.

title: The genetic history of the Southern Arc: A bridge between West Asia and Europe
authors: Lazaridis I., Alpaslan-Roodenberg S., Acar A., ... Reich D.
ask_addressed: Open and quote the primary aDNA and phylogenetic papers on Indo-European origins: Haak et al. 2015, Allentoft et al. 2015, Damgaard et al. 2018, Narasimhan et al. 2019, Bouckaert et al. 2012, Heggarty et al. 2023, Lazaridis et al. on the Anatolian question. Use bioRxiv, Europe PMC, PMC, institutional repositories, or Crossref/Unpaywall to find open copies.
quote: suggesting that the homeland of the Indo-Anatolian language family was in West Asia, with only secondary dispersals of non-Anatolian Indo-Europeans from the steppe.
summary: 727 ancient genomes from Anatolia and neighbours show Anatolia had negligible impact from later Yamnaya migrations, so the authors suggest a West Asian homeland for Indo-Anatolian, with Yamnaya a secondary dispersal.
limits: The paper states 'Language is not encoded in the genome'; the homeland claim is an inference from the absence of steppe ancestry in Anatolian-speaking regions, not a measurement. Several authors also wrote the 2015 steppe papers.

strand.what: Proto-Indo-Anatolian, splitting into Anatolian and Indo-European

authors: Lazaridis I., Nadel D., Rollefson G., ... Reich D.
ask_addressed: Open and quote the primary aDNA and phylogenetic papers on Indo-European origins: Haak et al. 2015, Allentoft et al. 2015, Damgaard et al. 2018, Narasimhan et al. 2019, Bouckaert et al. 2012, Heggarty et al. 2023, Lazaridis et al. on the Anatolian question. Use bioRxiv, Europe PMC, PMC, institutional repositories, or Crossref/Unpaywall to find open copies.
quote: farmers related to those from Iran spread northward into the Eurasian steppe
summary: 44 ancient Near Eastern genomes show Anatolian-related farmers spreading west into Europe and Iran-related farmers north into the steppe, which supplies the Near Eastern ancestry of the Yamnaya.
limits: Abstract gives no date for the northward spread; dates are broad. It bears on the Anatolian question only indirectly (it documents farmer ancestry in Europe, not language).

title: Do 'language trees with sampled ancestors' really support a 'hybrid model' for the origin of Indo-European? Thoughts on the most recent attempt at yet another IE phylogeny
ask_addressed: Quote each paper's own statement of what it shows and of its limits, and the strongest published criticisms.
quote: there remain serious issues when it comes to marking cognation between different characters
summary: Critique of Heggarty et al. 2023: data quality improved, but cognacy coding does not separate cognacy from areal diffusion, and the tree topology and datings contradict historical evidence in several ways.
limits: Authors belong to the 'Moscow school' and argue for a different method (intermediate reconstructions), so they have a stake. Does not itself support the steppe hypothesis.
